power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = 0.085", Sentence = "At follow-up, education remained strongly associated with BMI (p < 0.001), whereas gender no longer reached statistical significance (p = 0.085)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. text.text: Introduction: Socioeconomic differences in body mass index (BMI) are well established, but less is known about gender differences and their behavioral pathways.
We examined gender differences in the association between socioeconomic position (SEP) and BMI, and whether dietary factors and physical activity mediated the associations.
Methods: We used survey data from the employees of the City of Helsinki aged 19-39 collected in 2017 (n = 4,400, 80% women).

SEP was measured by highest educational attainment, and the examined mediators were consumption of fruit and vegetables, red and processed meat, sweets and confectionery and alcohol as well as leisure-time vigorous physical activity (VPA) and sedentary time.
We conducted gender-specific multiple mediation analyses using structural equation modeling and additional analyses using multiple imputation by chained equations.
Results: With increasing educational attainment, mean BMI decreased from 26.4 kg/m² to 24.0 kg/m² among women, and from 26.6 kg/m² to 25.2 kg/m² among men.
Lower SEP was associated with lower consumption of fruit and vegetables, higher consumption of red and processed meat, and lower VPA in both genders.
Women reported healthier diets but less VPA than men.

The strongest SEP-BMI mediator among women was VPA (indirect effect: 0.35, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.26, 0.44), followed by fruit and vegetable consumption (0.15, 95% CI 0.08, 0.23) and red and processed meat consumption (0.06, 95% CI 0.02, 0.11).
Among men, significant mediators were red and processed meat consumption (0.12, 95% CI 0.03, 0.23), sedentary time (0.11, 95% CI 0.01, 0.24) and VPA (0.10, 95% CI 0.02, 0.21).
Conclusions: Socioeconomic inequalities in BMI appear stronger among women and are shaped through partly different mechanisms between genders.
Improving VPA may be relevant among low-SEP women, whereas reducing sedentary time may be more relevant among low-SEP men.
Reducing red and processed meat is beneficial for both genders.

text.text: In high-income countries, body mass index (BMI) generally shows an inverse socioeconomic gradient, although the strength of this association differs by gender [7].

text.text: Previous studies have often reported stronger and more consistent inverse associations between SEP and obesity among women than among men [8, 9].

text.text: This pattern was already identified in the Finnish population in the 20 th century [10] and has since been replicated in later national and international studies [8, 11].

text.text: Dietary behaviors are among the most plausible mediators linking SEP to later BMI.
Lower SEP is linked to consuming fewer fruits and vegetables [12, 13].
text.formatted: Lower SEP is linked to consuming fewer fruits and vegetables <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13]</ref>.

text.text: Fruit and vegetable consumption can support weight regulation through lower energy density, higher fiber content and greater satiety, and previous research suggests a higher consumption is associated with reduced obesity [14].
text.formatted: Fruit and vegetable consumption can support weight regulation through lower energy density, higher fiber content and greater satiety, and previous research suggests a higher consumption is associated with reduced obesity <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref>.

text.text: By contrast, red and processed meats are often energy dense and embedded in dietary patterns associated with greater adiposity but have also been independently associated with weight gain [15].
text.formatted: By contrast, red and processed meats are often energy dense and embedded in dietary patterns associated with greater adiposity but have also been independently associated with weight gain <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>.

text.text: The consumption is higher in those with lower SEP, which makes it a potential mediator of the SEP-BMI association [12].
text.formatted: The consumption is higher in those with lower SEP, which makes it a potential mediator of the SEP-BMI association <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: Sweets and confectionery are also plausible mediators, although the strongest evidence linking sugar intake to obesity concerns sugar-sweetened beverages [16].
text.formatted: Sweets and confectionery are also plausible mediators, although the strongest evidence linking sugar intake to obesity concerns sugar-sweetened beverages <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref>.

text.text: Alcohol should also be considered, since it can contribute to excess energy intake directly or indirectly by weakening dietary restraint.
The epidemiological evidence on alcohol and adiposity is mixed, but heavier intake and some beverage patterns seem less favorable [17].
text.formatted: The epidemiological evidence on alcohol and adiposity is mixed, but heavier intake and some beverage patterns seem less favorable <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>.

text.text: However, no clear socioeconomic differences have been observed in sweets and confectionery or alcohol consumption, although the gender pattern suggests that women consume more sweets, whereas men consume more alcohol [12].

text.text: In addition to diet including alcohol consumption, moderate-to-vigorous physical activity as well as sedentary time are potential mediators since they are socioeconomically patterned, potentially modifiable and consistently linked to weight management [18] [19] [20].

text.text: Physical activity and less sedentary time may influence body weight not only through energy expenditure but also through improved appetite regulation and satiety signaling [21].

text.text: However, physical activity is socially patterned, and these patterns vary by domain and intensity: higher socioeconomic groups tend to be more active during leisure time and to accumulate more high-intensity physical activity, whereas lower socioeconomic groups tend to accumulate more occupational and light-intensity physical activity [19, 20, 22].

text.text: Sedentary time is positively associated with both general and abdominal obesity, and although sedentary time contributes to energy balance, the evidence is unclear whether increased sedentary time leads to increased BMI or whether the associations are due to reverse causation [23] [24] [25].

text.text: Socioeconomic differences also vary by sedentary domain, with higher SEP groups tending to report more occupational sitting, while lower SEP groups tend to report more leisure-time sitting [26].

text.text: Despite extensive research on socioeconomic differences in obesity, SEP-gender interactions in the associations are rarely explored.
More specifically, the mechanisms through which SEP contributes to the development of obesity, and whether these mechanisms differ by gender, remain insufficiently understood.

We hypothesize that lower SEP is linked to a higher BMI partly through dietary factors and physical activity and that the absolute effects of the mediators are larger among women because the SEP-obesity gradient is steeper in women.
First, we examined gender differences in the associations between SEP and BMI.
Second, we examined whether dietary factors and physical activity similarly mediate associations among both genders.

This study is part of the Helsinki Health Study, which examines the health and well-being of employees of the City of Helsinki, the largest employer in Finland with approximately 38,000 employees across diverse occupational sectors [27, 28].

text.text: The target population consisted of 11,459 employees born in 1978 or later (aged 19-39 years in 2017) who had been employed for at least four months with a contract of at least 50% regular working hours.
Data collection occurred in autumn 2017 (Phase 1) via online and mailed questionnaires, supplemented by shorter telephone interviews for non-responders.
The initial response rate was 51.5% (n = 5,898).
While non-response analysis indicated slightly higher participation among those with higher SEP, the sample was found to reasonably represent the target population [27].
text.formatted: While non-response analysis indicated slightly higher participation among those with higher SEP, the sample was found to reasonably represent the target population <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27]</ref>.

text.text: We excluded telephone interviewees (n = 510) because the interviews did not include all variables of interest needed for this study.
We also excluded those with missing data on education, BMI as well as one or more of the mediators, as shown in Figure 1.
text.formatted: We also excluded those with missing data on education, BMI as well as one or more of the mediators, as shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>.

text.text: Gender had no missing values.
Outliers in physical activity and sedentary time were identified as values more than three standard deviations from the mean, following previous studies [20].
text.formatted: Outliers in physical activity and sedentary time were identified as values more than three standard deviations from the mean, following previous studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref>.

text.text: The final analytical sample included 4,400 participants of whom 80% were women, reflecting the gender distribution of both the City of Helsinki and the broader Finnish municipal sector.
Two-thirds of the participants were aged 30-39 years, and one-third was aged 19-29 years.
Gender (male/female) was obtained from the surveys.

SEP was measured using the highest educational attainment, categorized into three groups: upper secondary or vocational education or lower (low), bachelor's degree (middle), and master's degree or higher (high).
BMI was computed from height and weight (kg/m²).

We included six behaviors, four related to diet: fruit and vegetable consumption, red and processed meat consumption, sweets and confectionery consumption, alcohol consumption, and two related to physical activity during leisure time: VPA and sedentary time.
These mediators were chosen because they are directly related to body weight through energy intake or energy expenditure.
Food consumption was assessed using a 14-item food frequency questionnaire (FFQ) covering the previous 4 weeks.
Consumption of fruit and vegetables was calculated by summing four items: fresh vegetables, fresh fruits, cooked vegetables, and berries.

Red and processed meat consumption was based on one questionnaire item, and sweets and confectionery consumption was calculated by summing two items, one on candy and chocolate and the other on coffee pastries and baked goods (biscuits/cookies, doughnuts, and other pastries).
The variables were divided by four to obtain weekly servings.

Alcohol consumption was assessed from participants' reported frequency of consuming three beverage types: beer, cider, long drink and similar beverages; wine and other lowalcohol beverages; and spirits or other strong alcoholic beverages.
Weekly alcohol consumption was calculated by summing the reported consumption frequencies across beverage types.
One unit of alcohol refers to 12 grams of pure ethanol.

Participants reported their leisure-time and commuting physical activity during the past 12 months by classifying activities according to perceived intensity and estimating the average weekly duration at each intensity level.
Intensity was converted to metabolic equivalents (METs) and multiplied by the duration of each intensity, following previous studies [29].
text.formatted: Intensity was converted to metabolic equivalents (METs) and multiplied by the duration of each intensity, following previous studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref>.

text.text: Only VPA (> 10 METs) was investigated as a mediator in the main analysis and total physical activity (sum of all the domains) in sensitivity analyses.
text.formatted: Only VPA (> 10 METs) was investigated as a mediator in the main analysis and total physical activity (sum of all the domains) in sensitivity analyses.

text.text: Sedentary time was assessed as self-reported daily sitting time across four domains: at home while watching television or using a computer, at home while reading, during transport, and elsewhere.
These were summed up and multiplied by seven to obtain time sitting per week.

If a participant reported physical activity, sedentary time or alcohol consumption for some domain but left one domain blank, the missing value for that domain was set to zero, following prior studies [19, 20].

text.text: Background characteristics of the participants were described by gender and SEP.
Continuous variables were presented as means and categorical variables as counts and percentages.
Age was categorized as 19-29 years and 30-39 years for descriptive analyses and treated as a continuous variable in mediation models, following previous studies [20].
text.formatted: Age was categorized as 19-29 years and 30-39 years for descriptive analyses and treated as a continuous variable in mediation models, following previous studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref>.

text.text: Differences in dietary factors and physical activity across gender and SEP groups were examined descriptively and visualized using bar plots.
The association between SEP and BMI was first examined visually and then tested using linear regression models.
Interaction terms between SEP and gender were used to assess whether educational differences in BMI differed between women and men.
Model assumptions, including the normality of residuals and heteroscedasticity, were assessed.

The mediating role of health dietary factors and physical activity in the association between SEP and BMI was examined using multiple parallel mediation models within a structural equation modeling framework in accordance with the conceptual model shown in Figure 2.
text.formatted: The mediating role of health dietary factors and physical activity in the association between SEP and BMI was examined using multiple parallel mediation models within a structural equation modeling framework in accordance with the conceptual model shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>.

text.text: All analyses were stratified by gender and adjusted for age.

A three-category SEP variable (upper secondary or vocational education or lower/bachelor's degree/master's degree or higher) was created for men and women separately, with the highest education being the reference group.
In each mediation model, SEP was specified as the exposure, BMI as the outcome, and dietary factors and physical activity as simultaneous mediators.
All mediators were treated as continuous variables.
The mediation analyses were conducted using structural equation modeling and followed the standard path-analytic approach [30].
text.formatted: The mediation analyses were conducted using structural equation modeling and followed the standard path-analytic approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref>.

text.text: First, the total association (c-path) between SEP and BMI was estimated.
Second, the associations between SEP and each mediator were estimated as a-paths.
Third, the associations between each mediator and BMI, adjusted for SEP and all other mediators, were estimated as b-paths.
The direct effect (c'-path) represented the association between SEP and BMI after adjustment for all mediators.
Mediator-specific indirect effects were calculated as the product of the corresponding a-and b-paths.
The total indirect effect was calculated as the sum of all mediator-specific indirect effects.
When the total effect (c-path) was statistically significant (p<0.05), the proportion mediated was calculated by dividing the indirect effect by the total effect.
text.formatted: When the total effect (c-path) was statistically significant (p<0.05), the proportion mediated was calculated by dividing the indirect effect by the total effect.

text.text: Indirect effects and confidence intervals were estimated using bootstrapped standard errors with 5,000 replications.
Model parameters are presented as non-standardized regression coefficients.
Nonstandardized estimates were used to allow more direct comparison between women and men, as the focus was on gender differences rather than comparisons between mediators within genders.
Standardized estimates depend on variable variances, which may differ by gender.
Results are reported separately for women and men as total effects, direct effects, total indirect effects and mediator-specific indirect effects.
Models were fitted using the lavaan package in R (version 4.5.3, 2026-03-11).
ChatGPT (OpenAI; accessed May 2025) was used to assist in generating R code for statistical analyses.
All AI-generated code was reviewed, tested, and modified as necessary by the authors, who verified the accuracy and reproducibility of the results.
A STROBE checklist is provided as a supplementary file (File S1).

To assess whether the observed mediation reflected socioeconomic differences in BMI already present at Phase 1, a secondary longitudinal analysis among those who had responded to the Phase 2 survey five years later in 2022 (n = 2581, 80% women) was conducted.
The cross-sectional analysis was chosen as the main analysis to maximize statistical power, as 40% of participants were lost to follow-up between Phases 1 and 2.
In the longitudinal model, Phase 2 BMI was used as the outcome variable, and the models were additionally adjusted for Phase 1 BMI.
Education was taken from Phase 2 to consider new completed education between Phase 1 and 2.

text.text: Women reported a higher consumption fruit and vegetables than men in all education groups, and in both genders, consumption decreased with lower education.
In contrast, red and processed meat consumption increased with decreasing education and was consistently higher among men than women.
Sweets and confectionery consumption was also higher among women than men, whereas alcohol consumption was higher among men across all education groups, with little difference by education.
VPA was higher among men than women and declined with decreasing education in both genders.
Sedentary time showed the opposite educational pattern, tending to be higher in the lower education groups, particularly among men.
Figure 4 shows an inverse association between SEP and BMI in both genders.

text.text: Among men, the gradient was relatively modest, whereas among women it was steeper, although men had a higher mean BMI overall.
Consequently, men had a higher BMI than women in the two higher education groups, but this gender difference narrowed in the lowest education group.

Statistical testing showed that both educational level and gender were associated with BMI (p < 0.001), and the education × gender interaction was statistically significant (p = 0.037), suggesting a gender difference in the association between SEP and BMI.

text.text: Compared to participants with high education, the total effect of middle education on BMI was similar in women and men, at 0.98 (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.61, 1.37) and 0.97 (95% CI 0.33, 1.61), respectively.

The association was stronger among participants with low education, particularly among women: compared with high education, the total effect of low education on BMI was 2.84 (95% CI 2.34, 3.35) in women and 1.67 (95% CI 0.99, 2.34) in men.

In both women and men, compared with those with high education, the middle and low education groups had significantly lower consumption of fruit and vegetables, higher consumption of red and processed meat, and lower VPA, as shown by the a-paths in Table 2.

text.text: In addition, lower education was associated with lower alcohol consumption among women, and with higher sedentary time and lower sweets consumption among men.
Lower education was also associated with lower sweets and confectionery consumption among women and lower alcohol consumption among men.
Higher consumption of fruit and vegetables was associated with lower BMI only among women, whereas higher VPA was associated with lower BMI in both genders, shown as the b-paths in Table 2.

text.text: In contrast, higher red and processed meat consumption and greater sedentary time were associated with higher BMI among both women and men.
The associations of VPA and sedentary time with BMI were stronger among women, whereas the association between red and processed meat and BMI was stronger among men.
Sweets and confectionery and alcohol consumption were not significantly associated with BMI in either gender.

Among women, VPA showed the largest indirect effect, both for middle versus high education (0.18, 95% CI 0.11, 0.26; 18.6% mediated) and low versus high education (0.35, 95% CI 0.26, 0.44; 12.1% mediated).

Smaller indirect effects were observed through consumption of fruit and vegetables among women (middle vs high: 0.05, 95% CI 0.01, 0.09; 4.8% mediated; low vs high: 0.15, 95% CI 0.08, 0.23; 5.4% mediated) and through consumption of red and processed meat in both women (middle vs high: 0.04, 95% CI 0.01, 0.07; 3.9% mediated; low vs high: 0.06, 95% CI 0.02, 0.11; 2.1% mediated) and men (middle vs high: 0.09, 95% CI 0.01, 0.19; 9.2% mediated; low vs high: 0.12, 95% CI 0.03, 0.23; 7.2% mediated).

Among men, additional significant indirect pathways were observed through sedentary time (middle vs high: 0.09, 95% CI 0.01, 0.22; 9.3% mediated; low vs high: 0.11, 95% CI 0.01, 0.24; 6.3% mediated) and, for the low versus high education comparison, through VPA (0.10, 95% CI 0.02, 0.21; 5.3% mediated).

Red and processed meat consumption showed larger absolute and relative indirect effects in men than in women, whereas no clear indirect effects were observed for sweets and confectionery consumption or alcohol consumption in either gender.

Taken together, all mediators explained 29.0% of the education-BMI association among women in the middle versus high education comparison and 20.1% in the low versus high comparison; among men, the corresponding proportions were 26.8% and 25.3%, respectively.

text.text: Among women, mean BMI increased by 1.1 kg/m² in the high education group, 1.3 kg/m² in the middle education group, and 1.3 kg/m² in the low education group, reaching 25.4 kg/m², 26.0 kg/m², and 28.5 kg/m² in 2022, respectively.

Among men, mean BMI increased by 0.7 kg/m² in the high education group, 0.9 kg/m² in the middle education group, and 0.9 kg/m² in the low education group, reaching 26.0 kg/m², 27.3 kg/m², and 28.0 kg/m² in 2022, respectively.
Thus, BMI increased over follow-up in all education groups, but the highest BMI levels were consistently observed in the low education group, and the increase was more pronounced among women.
The categorical BMI distribution showed a similar development, with the proportion of overweight and obesity increasing and normal weight decreasing.

text.text: The a-paths showed a broadly similar pattern with lower educational level being still associated with lower consumption of fruit and vegetables and higher red and processed meat consumption.

Lower sweets and confectionery consumption and more sedentary time were associated with lower education in men, whereas lower alcohol consumption and less VPA were associated with lower education in women.

However, the b-paths linking the mediators to follow-up BMI were clearly weaker than in the crosssectional model with only red and processed meat consumption remaining positively associated with follow-up BMI among women and fruit and vegetable and sweets and confectionery consumption in men.
Accordingly, the indirect effects were small and inconsistent.
Among women, there was some evidence of mediation through red and processed meat consumption and through VPA.
Among men, the significant indirect effects were observed for consumption of fruit and vegetables and sweets and confectioneries.
The summed indirect effects across all mediators were not statistically significant in any group.
Since the total effects of SEP on Phase 2 BMI were not statistically significant, the mediated proportions were not calculated.

The longitudinal model adjusting for baseline BMI suggests that the educational differences in BMI were present already at Phase 1 and that Phase 2 BMI was largely explained by prior BMI rather than by subsequent BMI change.
Our main finding was that the association between SEP and BMI was stronger among women than among men, and that this difference was partly explained by dietary factors and physical activity.
Consumption of red and processed meat was an important mediator in both genders, although it explained a larger part of the SEP-BMI association among men.
VPA was the most prominent mediator among women, followed by consumption of fruit and vegetables.
Sedentary time was a significant mediator only among men, while alcohol and sweets and confectionery consumption did not mediate the SEP-BMI association in either gender.
Additional analyses with 5-year follow-up BMI adjusted for baseline BMI suggested that educational differences in follow-up BMI were largely explained by baseline BMI instead of the mediators.
The steeper SEP-BMI gradient in women than in men has been well established in previous literature, both in the Finnish population and internationally [8, 11].

text.text: Because we used education as the SEP indicator in this study, it remains to be seen whether the observed gender differences in SEP-BMI association would be equally consistent if other SEP indicators were used.
Lower SEP was associated with a less favorable behavioral profile in both genders, including lower consumption of fruit and vegetables, higher consumption of red and processed meat, and lower VPA.

The educational differences in diet quality were in line with the Finnish national dietary surveys [12] as well as international evidence, where the clearest support is seen for fruit and vegetable consumption [13, 35].

text.text: Because our study measured only leisure-time vigorous activity, the observed socioeconomic patterning may reflect the possibility that lower educated individuals accumulate more occupational physical activity and less occupational sedentary time, whereas higher educated individuals engage more in leisuretime physical activity but may also have more sedentary work.
Additionally, gender differences related to dietary factors and physical activity were consistent with prior national and international evidence [12, 37, 38].

text.text: However, that study had a 13-year follow-up, during which educational differences in BMI gain were detected.
It is therefore possible that our 5-year follow-up was too short to detect clear differences in BMI change.
BMI increased rather similarly across educational groups, so adjusting for baseline BMI largely attenuated the educational differences.
Regarding the study population, this study used a large occupational cohort of young adults aged 19-39 years, including both manual and non-manual employees.
However, the sample was mostly women (80%), which likely reduced statistical power in the male subgroup and may partly explain why some associations among men were not statistically significant.

Although the data may be generalized with caution to the working-age Finnish population, they cannot be directly generalized to the entire adult population because the cohort consisted only of employees of the City of Helsinki.
Thus, a healthy worker effect is likely, and the lowest SEP group in this study does not represent the most socioeconomically disadvantaged groups in society, such as the long-term unemployed [44].

Self-reported height and weight may introduce bias, although they are generally considered sufficiently accurate for epidemiological research [46, 47].

text.text: The dietary measure was based on a short FFQ that was not formally validated and did not include portion sizes, meaning that absolute consumption could not be estimated.

However, short FFQs have been shown to be suitable for assessing group-level differences in frequently consumed foods [49, 50] and portion-size questions may contribute relatively little to variance in intake [51].

text.text: Regarding statistical analysis, our cross-sectional design does not allow for causal conclusions.
We conducted a follow-up analysis, but it did not completely overcome this limitation because dietary factors and physical activity were measured at the same time as SEP.
Additionally, the follow-up sample was smaller and more selective.
We also adjusted the mediation models only for age, so some residual confounding may remain.
However, the statistical framework of structural equation is built on the previous findings suggesting a causal relationship between SEP and BMI through health behaviors.
Our results suggest that socioeconomic differences in BMI are not explained by a single behavioral pathway, but rather by a myriad of factors, with some mechanisms being gender specific.
For example, improving VPA may be relevant among low-SEP women, whereas reducing sedentary time may be more relevant among low-SEP men.
At the same time, consumption of red and processed meat emerged as a common pathway in both genders.
The stronger SEP-BMI gradient observed among women suggests that women in lower SEP may be more vulnerable to weight gain, so health policies should focus on this group.

Because these six mediators explained only about one quarter of the SEP-BMI association, the findings indicate the importance of other mechanisms, including psychosocial stress, neighborhood environment, working conditions and access to healthy food and exercise opportunities being potential mediators of the SEP-BMI association.
Future research is needed to identify additional mediators of the SEP-BMI association to better understand why the association is more pronounced in women.
Future studies would also benefit from repeated measurements of both mediators and BMI, so that changes over time and causal pathways could be examined more clearly.
Taken together, our findings suggest that different behavioral mechanisms may underlie socioeconomic differences in BMI in men and women.

VPA and fruit and vegetable consumption were significant mediators of the SEP-BMI association in women and sedentary time in men, while red and processed meat intake acted as a mediator in both genders.
The association between SEP and BMI was stronger among women than among men, and the 5-year increase in BMI was more pronounced in women, especially among those with the lowest education.
These results suggest that prevention of weight gain and the reduction of SEP-related health inequalities should focus on gender-specific approaches.

At the same time, because only about one quarter of the SEP-BMI association was explained by the included dietary factors and physical activity patterns, broader structural, social, and environmental factors are likely to play an important role in maintaining weight-related inequalities.
